articles.raw_content:
UK roads risk being left gridlocked by immovable buses with built-in ‘kill switches’ if councils ramp up purchases of cheaper Chinese electric vehicles to replace ageing fleets, a leading security figure has warned.



Hundreds of Chinese electric buses, which can be remotely deactivated by on-board SIM cards, have already been purchased by UK councils in a bid to meet financial and environmental pressures.



Security experts fear the influx will gather pace following the Government’s decision to devolve more spending powers to councils, which are increasingly attracted to the lower cost of Chinese vehicles compared to Western counterparts. 



Luke de Pulford, co-founder of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, said more regional spending decisions are likely to result in “an increasing amount of the purchasing of risky Chinese tech outsourced to councils”.





He said: “As we move towards a greener economy, there is heavy pressure on public authorities to procure green vehicles,” adding that lower prices will put “pressure upon local authorities to get them from Chinese sources”.



“We’ll be talking buses used to transport senior citizens and everybody else.”



Security fears over components in Chinese EVs have seen such vehicles banned by the Ministry of Defence over spying concerns, while the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) found it was “technically possible” for electric buses from China already on Britain’s roads to be remotely stopped by Beijing.

At least two other shadow fleet tankers appear to have been following Myra’s path, according to analysis by The i Paper, with the sanctioned Rora and Leruo both circumnavigating the UK instead of going through the Channel after departing Russian port Primorsk.  
False alarm, but a real threat 
The scale of the danger of the situation subsided after those on board later said the distress call had been a false alarm and continued on their route towards Spain. 
It has not been confirmed whether the ship was carrying fuel, as would be expected for a tanker departing Ust Luga and destined for Port Said in Egypt, but open-source analysis suggests the vessel appears to be empty or only part-loaded.

articles.jina_text:
The UK Government wants to see the Acorn carbon capture and storage project succeed, a UK minister has said, after concerns were raised about the way it is being funded.




The project in Aberdeenshire was due to receive £200 million in grant funding from the UK Government, but Chancellor John Healey changed the commitment to mean the UK Government would offer the same amount in loans or receive an equity stake in the project.








Scotland’s First Minister John Swinney has said he was “deeply concerned” about changes to the funding mechanism.




Acorn, which could support about 15,000 jobs at its peak, proposes storing emissions from across Scotland under the seabed of the North Sea.


(PA Graphics)
PA Graphics




UK Government energy minister Martin McCluskey said it had been necessary to “reprioritise” budgets to prioritise investing in defence, but that the UK Government wanted to support the project.




He told The Sunday Show on the BBC: “We awarded £200 million in grant funding at the last spending review.




“Some of that has already been drawn down by the developers, and the money that they’ve already drawn down remains in place.













“For the remainder, and for any future support, instead of it being through grant funding, it will be through loans and equities.




“Why are we doing that? We’re doing that for two reasons. Firstly, loans and equities are better value for the taxpayer. It means that perhaps we could choose to take a stake in that project, which would give a return to the taxpayer.









“But second, we’ve had to make some really difficult choices to reprioritise within budgets in order to fund the defence investment plan, which is obviously a priority for the Government.”




Mr McCluskey said the UK Government has had to “reprioritise” carbon capture and storage programmes right across the UK, and that a number of programmes have actually been stopped, not just reprioritised in terms of loans and equities.

‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets


Cop17, focused on protecting nature and restoring ecosystems, concludes on Saturday with critics saying system allows ‘one idiot’ to stall progress




Calls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the destruction of the natural world, with governments likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the convention.
Two weeks of negotiations at biodiversity Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded on Saturday morning with countries vowing to redouble their efforts to meet this decade’s targets, which include commitments to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore nearly a third of Earth’s degraded ecosystems and reform $500bn (£410bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies.

Agreed just four years ago by nearly every government on the planet, they aim to transform humanity’s relationship with nature. Despite progress in some areas, governments are way off track on meeting almost all of the targets. The UK is set to meet just three of the 23.
After talks that ran overnight from Friday into Saturday morning, countries signed off several measures, including a commitment to ramp up action on meeting existing targets and reaffirming a goal to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade.
During the conference, environment ministers, activists and officials appealed for significant changes to the way the summits function to ensure governments follow through with meaningful action on the drivers of biodiversity loss.
Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, a veteran conservationist, said the Cop process had been “designed to fail”, arguing that decisions should be taken by a majority as the consensus-based process allows “one idiot” to prevent agreement.
“A lot of what’s going on out here at the Cop is just a bunch of baloney and beautiful speeches and BS,” he told AFP earlier this week. “We cannot have – we cannot expect – a consensus between every nation on Earth on every topic. That’s ridiculous. Cops have been designed to fail, and they are not disappointing.”

Healey to veto new offshore wind projects if they will not lower bills


UK chancellor’s plans add to concerns government is moving away from pro-renewables agenda




John Healey has said he will veto new offshore wind projects if they will not lower bills, adding to concerns that the government is moving away from the pro-renewables agenda.
Announcing his plans, the chancellor said clean power is “how we break the grip of international gas prices on our bills”, but added the shift towards it “has to come at the right pace, in the right places, with the grid to carry it”.

New offshore wind projects lodging bids for subsidy contracts will only get signed off by ministers if they believe that all the power generated could be accommodated by Britain’s electricity grid without pushing up costs for consumers.
Writing in the Times, he said: “There’s no sense building power that can’t connect and then paying to switch it off. We will take that approach into our next renewables auction, only buying projects that can lower bills while strengthening our energy security.”

articles.jina_text:
John Swinney has said he is “deeply concerned” by the decision to cancel grant funding for an “absolutely central” carbon capture and storage (CCS) facility.




The Acorn project in Aberdeenshire was due to receive £200 million in grant funding from the UK Government, but Chancellor John Healey changed the commitment to mean the UK Government would offer the same amount in loans or receive an equity stake in the project.








UK ministers were accused of causing confusion over the funding this week, with Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds telling the BBC: “There hasn’t been a cut to the £200 million, I can reassure you that that commitment stands.




“That is the grant funding, but there could well be loans or equity stakes taken, because we will need probably additional funding to secure the future of this project.”




Speaking to the Press Association on Friday, the First Minister voiced his opposition to the decision.




“I raised the issue of Acorn and my concerns about the fact that I think further uncertainty has been created for Acorn,” he said.













“What I understand the position to be is the UK Government has decided not to offer grant funding to the Acorn project, but instead to do that through financial transactions.




“That creates more risk, that creates more uncertainty about the project.




“The very act of changing the funding mechanism does that, and I am deeply concerned about that because I think the Acorn project is an absolutely central project in relation to our work on climate action and it’s essential that it’s taken forward as part of that agenda and as part of encouraging the reindustrialisation of Scotland.”









A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson said: “We recognise Acorn’s role in supporting good, well-paid jobs and reindustrialisation in Scotland.




“Acorn will continue to receive its existing grant funding until the end of the year.




“Future support will be through loans or equity stakes that need to see the taxpayer receive a return.

UK politics live – latest updates  




The leader of the UK’s biggest trade union has called for the same political focus to be given to NHS, education and care sector workers as there has been on those employed in North Sea oil and gas.
Andrea Egan, the general secretary of Unison, said that too often public sector workers were treated as an “afterthought” by the government compared with the “massive political focus” on protecting jobs in the North Sea.

“There’s no question it is vital for oil and gas workers to be guaranteed secure, well-paid jobs in the industries of the future,” Egan said. “But public service workers, in contrast, often seem like an afterthought for ministers. What about the thousands of jobs cut in recent years across local government, the NHS and education? Care workers, nurses, teaching assistants.”


North Sea oil and gas has been in the headlines again in recent weeks after the government gave the go ahead to the Jackdaw gasfield following huge pressure from the fossil fuel industry and rightwing politicians – in the UK and abroad.







Burnham in danger of sleepwalking into climate disaster, say campaigners

The decision was met with anger by climate campaigners and scientists, as well as many Labour supporters, who argue that extracting more fossil fuels will drive the escalating crisis and do nothing to reduce bills, significantly improve energy security or halt the long-term decline in jobs in the sector. A final government decision on the more controversial Rosebank oilfield is expected before the end of the year.
After Wednesday’s budget, the forecasts for which factored in the project’s approval, the Guardian revealed some Labour MPs are lobbying Andy Burnham and John Healey not to overrule the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, if she decides to block Rosebank.
But Egan said approving Jackdaw was “a serious misstep from the government” and sent the wrong signal about the UK’s climate commitments. Instead, she said ministers should focus on creating secure, well-paid jobs in the renewable sector for oil and gas workers and give similar support to the millions of people who work in the public sector which has also been hit by severe cuts in recent years.

articles.raw_rss: The effects of El Niño could be felt in the capital as early as November, forecasters warn

articles.jina_text:
Londoners could face freezing temperatures far sooner than expected, as El Niño continues to strengthen across the Pacific to what some scientists are calling “unprecedented levels”.




Forecasters have warned that the global phenomenon could disrupt the polar vortex – a vast ring of freezing winds high above the Arctic that normally keeps the coldest air contained around the North Pole.








Should the vortex weaken, it could disrupt the jet stream, allowing bitterly cold Arctic air to plunge southwards towards Europe.




And the impact could be felt across the capital as early as November, with London facing a sudden drop in temperatures months earlier than previously expected.




It was initially anticipated that temperatures would drop in January of next year. 


Londoners could face freezing temperatures far sooner than expected this winter
PA Wire




But NASA forecasts show the wind circulation weakening, with wind strength falling to 26.9mph on October 31, to 20.5mph on November 1 and 9.3mph on November 3. 




The development has raised questions over what it could mean for winter in the UK, particularly as forecasters monitor the possibility of a sudden stratospheric warming event.








“The stratospheric sudden warming can sometimes cause the jet stream to ‘snake’ more, and this tends to create a large area of blocking high pressure,” the forecaster said.













Experts say this weather pattern typically develops over the North Atlantic and Scandinavia, bringing the prospect of prolonged periods of cold, dry weather across northern Europe, including the UK.




Meanwhile, southern parts of Europe are more likely to experience milder, wetter and windier conditions.


People in snowy conditions in Westminster central London
PA Wire




Along the boundary of these areas, easterly winds can develop, dragging colder air westwards. 




In some cases, the plunge in temperatures can bring snowfall as seen during the severe cold spell of early 2018, infamously known as the 'Beast from the East'.









But forecasters can only reliably predict sudden stratospheric warmings around a week in advance. 




The chances of an atmospheric disruption are unusually high this year. Meteorological models are currently tracking an imminent, potentially record-breaking event, with forecasting odds sitting between 61% and 86% for a major stratospheric disturbance.




Dr Judah Cohen, an atmospheric and environmental research scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), told Fox Weather: “This will be, I think almost undoubtedly, the largest, earliest disruption of the polar vortex on record.”


London is set for a particularly wet and stormy winter as a result of El Nino
AFP/Getty




Government officials and emergency campaigns, such as the 'Be Ready' initiative, have urged households to stockpile a three-day to two-week supply of essential items to prepare for severe disruptions brought about by the extreme weather.

There was a warmer response to the decision to scrap standing charges on gas.

Anger at the “ridiculously expensive” price of fuel and the cost of food were his main concerns.

Busy California airports used by millions of travelers could face flooding risks during the upcoming holiday season thanks to sea level rise and a record-breaking El Niño climate pattern, a new report warns. 
While recent levee improvements have reduced the risk at Oakland International Airport, San Francisco International Airport - built on marshland - is vulnerable to flooding of 3 feet or more. Full SummaryClimate scientists from the University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab warn that a Super El Niño could cause nearly 900,000 additional heat-related deaths globally over a 10-month period. The phenomenon is expected to hit countries like Nigeria, India, and China the hardest, with researchers linking the increasing strength of El Niño events to human-caused climate change.
Super El Niño could lead to nearly 900,000 extra deaths worldwide over just 10 months, climate scientists have warned in an alarming new prediction. 
The El Niño Heat Mortality Tracker, produced by the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab, forecasts the human impact of the weather phenomenon. El Niño occurs when the average sea surface temperatures in the central and tropical Pacific Ocean rise above the long-term average by 2C or more.
Researchers estimate the climate pattern has already lead to 484,500 excess heat-related deaths between June and September this year, with around 372,900 more forecast for the next six months. 




The mortality tracker map gives a breakdown of which countries are most badly affected, with Nigeria expected to see the highest death toll. Experts predict the African nation will see more than 56,000 additional deaths across the next six months, according to Climate Impact Lab.

articles.jina_text:
South West Water has been given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency over high levels of pollution.
The regulator downgraded the firm from two stars out of a possible four to one, meaning it is now considered a "poor performing company" for its environmental impact.
It said it had performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents for the 15th year in a row.
South West Water, which has 1.8 million customers across Devon, Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and parts of Dorset and Somerset, said it knew there was "much more to do" and was taking action to improve areas that "matter most" to customers and the environment.
The annual Environmental Performance Assessment grades England's nine water and sewerage companies largely on how often they pollute rivers, streams and the sea.
For 2025, South West Water was among four companies rated as poor performing, or one star, while four others were rated as requiring improvement, two stars.


South West Water performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents
Severn Trent Water was the only company to achieve the highest rating of four stars.














The Environment Agency's report card comes a month after South West Water was fined almost £8m for a series of pollution-related offences over six years.
In the last year it also recorded the sharpest rise in customer complaints of any water company.
Serious incidents in the past year include pollution in St Austell River, killing thousands of fish, while pollution at Exmouth meant beachgoers had to leave the water.
Industry regulator Ofwat said the company met seven of its 23 targets in 2025-26, with below target performance for "most areas".
It noted its performance in relation to water supply interruptions "deteriorated substantially" and, despite improving annual performance by 38%, said the company's total pollution incidents performance remained more than double its target.
Customer satisfaction also remained challenging, ranking 15 out of 17 in the sector.
While storm overflows performance improved by 19%, it still fell short of its target, the Environment Agency said.

articles.title: Mini-gardens for bees on bus stop roofs approved

articles.raw_meta: Living Roofs aimed at boosting biodiversity in urban areas will be installed under a new bus stop contract.
articles.jina_text:
Peterborough City Council said 34 bus stops could include Living Roofs, mini-gardens planted on top of bus shelters that are made up of wildflowers and other vegetation.
The initiative was included in its new plan for the city's bus stops, which will also see "comfortable seating" replace existing perch seats.
At a meeting of the cabinet, external on Tuesday, the plans were discussed and approved.
The council will award a new contract to Bauer Media Outdoor UK to manage the city's bus stops.
The agreement includes the company providing the council with an annual income of £140,000 from the sale of advertising space, plus 2.5% of its quarterly gross revenue.
The contract is expected to run for a minimum of 10 years, with options to extend it, and could provide the authority with £2.8m over 20 years.
There are more than 350 Living Roofs across the UK, including in Birmingham, Glasgow and Northampton.
Chris Wiggin, the council's Liberal Democrat cabinet member for environment, said: "We need to do everything we can to support biodiversity and support bees and other pollinators because without those there is no other life, so I'm very happy to see these [plans] come forward."
Other planned changes to the city's bus stops include providing up-to-date passenger information and installing digital advertising screens at most bus stops.

A majestic tract of land in far north Queensland that links wet tropics and world heritage rainforest, and contains headwaters that flow to the Great Barrier Reef, could be bought and protected by Christmas, after a conservation group raised more than $19m in private donations to buy the cattle station.


Wooroora spans more than 20,000 hectares of largely intact wet sclerophyll forest and savanna woodland on the lands of the Jirrbal people about 100km south-west of Cairns – and borders Bush Heritage’s existing 43,575-hectare Yourka Reserve in one of the most biodiverse regions in Australia.
Cassowary and tree-kangaroos are among at least 12 threatened species and more than 30 species of conservation significance that have already been recorded on Wooroora, which is also the northernmost refuge for koalas, and, according to the would-be owners, is almost certainly home to species yet unknown to science.

Wooroora station is the most northerly habitat for koalas.  Photograph: John Wybrow

The chief executive of Bush Heritage, Rachel Lowry, said Wooroora would be the organisation’s most ambitious single acquisition in its 35-year history to date.
“This breaks the glass ceiling,” Lowry said. “And I don’t think it’s just for Bush Heritage, but for our sector more broadly.”
Lowry said fundraising for the $24.7m to buy and manage the land for an initial five years has been going on for more than 18 months. She travelled to New York during the 2025 UN climate summit to make a presentation that helped result in a donation of almost $2.5m from the foundation associated with the US outdoor clothing company Patagonia.

‘We’re leaving a legacy worldwide’ … Bush Heritage Australia’s chief executive, Rachel Lowry.


Given the country is a global biodiversity hotspot, Lowry said the protection “forever” of Wooroora was “not just a gift for Australia”.
“When we step in and we protect and manage country, like Wooroora, we’re leaving a legacy worldwide,” she said.
An anonymous Australian philanthropist also donated $6m. Now Bush Heritage is appealing to the public to raise the final $5.3m it needs by the deadline of 24 December.

The UK has only succeeded in meeting a key international climate finance target through “questionable accounting”, new research claims – as climate-vulnerable countries look to pile new pressure on rich countries to stump up more cash at the upcoming Cop31 climate conference.
As part of its obligations under the Paris Agreement, the UK pledged to give at least £11.6 billion in international “climate finance” between 2021 and 2026.

The radical Stern report showed that a low-carbon future is also good economics. But it seems that capitalism needs a reminder




Saving the only planet we have makes good economic sense. There is, after all, no money to be made on a dead Earth. There may be costs involved now, but they are worth paying to protect our children from certain destruction.
These propositions seem self-evident now. But two decades ago, mainstream economists had very different ideas. They had proved that the climate crisis would be a mere economic blip, easily absorbed by growing economies and therefore not worth spending money on. In their accounting, they considered ice caps and glaciers functionally worthless, that trees only add to GDP when they are cut down, and that a livable climate shouldn’t even merit a line on a spreadsheet.

What changed? Twenty years ago this week an earth-shaking report was published by Nicholas Stern, a former World Bank chief economist turned adviser to Gordon Brown. His review, The Economics of Climate Change, upended conventional wisdom among economists and dragged them into a new century. It set out, for the first time, in clear and bold terms, why investing in a low-carbon future makes economic sense.


The Stern review, in 700 dense pages full of graphs and data, is a model of transformative thinking. Using standard economic tools and methods, and in ways that other mainstream economists could understand, Stern made three key, and at the time radical, conclusions: that the costs of inaction on the climate were greater than the costs of action; that the climate crisis was a market failure; and that economic growth was compatible with cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
Stern’s crucial insight, the revolutionary idea on which his whole thesis turned, was that future generations have as much right to be born as we did. Traditional economics mistrusts anything that could happen in the future, applying a “discount rate” to it. Likely future profits are reckoned as lower in value than those of the present, as are likely future losses.

A Freedom of Information (FoI) request by Fast Loan UK to Transport for London (TfL) shows that over 1.6 million penalty charge notices (PCNs) were issued in the capital between April 1, 2025, and March 31, 2026.








The 1,683,552 total charges equate to around 4,612 notices per day, 192 per hour, or 3.2 per minute across the year.




Despite the huge figures, the number of PCNs has actually fallen 13.9% from the previous financial year, when 1,956,441 ULEZ penalty notices were issued by TfL.




May 2025 saw the most PCNs, with 158,528 notices issued - equating to a staggering 5,110 fines per day - while July saw 156,030 PCNs and February recorded the lowest total at 118,626.




Despite the large figures, around 72% of the challenges made to TfL were accepted.




TfL recorded 117,275 accepted representations and 45,567 rejected representations in 2025/26, with a further 754 remaining open.













Earlier this year, Sadiq Khan hailed the impact of ULEZ expansion amid claims that toxic air-related deaths fell by as much as 40%.




The Mayor of London implemented the Ulez scheme across inner London in October 2021, and expanded it across the whole of the city in August 2023, establishing the world’s largest pollution charging zone.









A study from Imperial College London’s environmental research group estimated that premature deaths attributable to air quality in London was 3,800 to 5,100 in 2024, down from 6,400 to 8,000 in 2019.




The study was commissioned by the Greater London Authority and Transport for London.




Commenting on the report at the time, Sir Sadiq said: “The evidence is now overwhelming and unarguable: the bold action we have taken in London has reduced pollution, improved public health and saved lives.”

Households across the UK can now cut their energy bills by hundreds of pounds a year at no upfront cost by applying for interest-free or “low-interest” loans to fund upgrades such as heat pumps, batteries and solar panels.
The government-backed Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, could mean thousands more households are able to access low-carbon energy alternative technologies, thanks to loans ranging from £7,500 to up £35,000.

Energy suppliers including British Gas and E.On have partnered with lenders from Tandem Bank and Homeserve respectively to offer the loans directly to customers at a discounted rate compared with those offered by high street lenders.



People interested in swapping their gas boiler for an air-source or ground-source heat pump could secure loans of up to £10,000 or £35,000 respectively, while also drawing on the government’s existing scheme which offers grants of up to £9,000 a year for households installing the replacements for fossil fuel heating.

Installing a heat pump, battery and solar panels could save households up to £550 a year on their energy bills, rising by a further £300 a year with a time-of-use tariff, according to the government.

Trump’s cuts have exposed US to ‘cascade’ of El Niño dangers, experts warn


President has taken an axe to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, stalling climate research on and response to extreme weather events




Sweeping cuts to the premier US climate agency under Donald Trump have severely hampered the country’s capacity to forecast, research and respond to extreme weather events, former government officials and scientists have warned, as the US faces a cascade of hazards fueled by a potentially historic El Niño this winter.
From the start of his second term, the president has taken aim at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), slashing staff levels, canceling contracts and grants, and shutting down databases and research laboratories. The agency that has long been considered a global crown jewel in climate science and forecasting, has lost roughly 20% of its staff since January 2025.

The National Weather Service, which is housed within Noaa, has also taken a hit. Weather stations have had to delay data collection and cut operating hours, with hundreds of meteorological and other technical positions still vacant across its 122 forecast offices.

The effects have already been felt at Noaa, where a chaotic and volatile environment has plummeted morale, increased burnout and hampered vital work. While capacity has quietly unravelled, a large-scale disaster will quickly expose the most dangerous gaps.


“The system has not really been tested since all the cuts happened,” said Tom Di Liberto, a former Noaa climate scientist who now works as the media director of Climate Central.
That test could soon be coming.
This year’s super El Niño, a climate phenomenon characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the ability to fuel extreme weather events around the world. It’s already climbing off the charts and is expected to strengthen through the northern hemisphere’s autumn and winter.
Along with dangerous spikes in temperature, El Niño will supercharge storms in parts of the American west, raise sea levels in California by up to a foot, and set the stage for debris flows, land slides and flash floods.
“Whether we as a country can handle the kind of coast-to-coast extremes that could potentially happen this winter is a big question,” Di Liberto said.

Super-rich get ‘double dividend’ from causes and costs of climate crisis, report finds


Oxfam says investing by rich in disaster recovery widens inequality and gives incentive to delay climate action




The world’s wealthiest people are not just profiting from the polluting causes of climate breakdown, they are also increasingly cashing in on the catastrophic consequences, according to a study by Oxfam.
The global equality organisation has found that the richest 0.1% of the world’s population are heavily invested in disaster preparedness, recovery and reconstruction – a market that is projected to grow from $70bn to $92bn a year by 2029.

This gives the planet’s wealthiest and most powerful people a “double dividend” from the climate crisis and, more alarmingly, an incentive to delay or disrupt action to solve the problem, the NGO says.
It also worsens global inequality as those least responsible for global heating end up having to pay those most responsible in terms of higher food prices, repairing homes damaged by extreme weather or relocating to other areas.


Jean McLean, Oxfam’s chief influencing officer, accused billionaires of turning chaos into profit. “The super-rich benefit at both ends of the crisis: first, through continued investment in polluting industries, and second, through investment in the booming ‘adaptation economy’ – recovery and rebuilding services are sold back to a warming world,” she said.
“The populations who contributed least to the climate crisis are absorbing its worst consequences, while those who caused it are best equipped to protect themselves.”
The richest 0.1% on the planet, a group of 8 million people, are responsible for more carbon emissions than the poorest 3.5 billion combined, the report says. As a result, this group have reportedly contributed by 125 times more than the average person to extreme heat events.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days
articles.raw_rss: From Brexit debates to North Sea oil, there is plenty getting the cabinet, the Labour Party and the country talking.

articles.jina_text:
It is now 100 days since Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street from Buckingham Palace and began to assemble his cabinet. 
Three months later, Labour MPs are more chipper, the party's poll ratings have notched up and the tone and style of government feels very different from when Sir Keir Starmer was in charge.
Coming next, though, there are a whole series of crunchy decisions and trade offs – economic and political – some of which are inevitable and some of which Burnham has decided to lean into.
First up, the Budget
You would be forgiven for only just clocking there is a Budget this week. 
There are three reasons for this year's feeling like a comparatively low key affair: it is happening a month earlier than a year ago, squeezing the space available for briefings, leaks and speculation. It is considerably smaller in big picture terms – in other words the scale of tax rises – so limiting the noisy talk in advance about who might get clobbered. And the new chancellor John Healey and his team have sought to make a virtue out of not saying very much beforehand.
But woe betide suggesting to anyone involved in assembling this Budget that it is a steady-as-she-goes, nothing-to-see-here thing.














Every Budget is a big deal, goes the argument run past me by some. They don't all have to be visible from space in the way some recent ones have been – think Kwasi Kwarteng in one direction followed by Jeremy Hunt in the other four years ago, or Rachel Reeves in the last two years.
Cost of living support for some, help for entrepreneurs, more financial clout for mayors in England and an economy now recuperating will be themes for Healey on Wednesday.
You will be the judge of this Budget's scale – its value, or the lack of it to you – before long.
Next, Brexit – and our relationship with the EU
In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too close and, if needs must, climb over it gingerly.
Burnham has no such reservations: he has repeatedly said in the last few weeks, let's talk about Brexit. He reckons the current deal between the UK and European Union isn't good enough.
Over the weekend he went further, suggesting he wanted an "honest discussion" about freedom of movement. Countries in the EU's single market have to sign up to freedom of movement, which lets people live and work in all the countries that are part of it. Given how big a deal immigration was for many in the EU referendum in 2016, even reopening the question of freedom of movement feels like a big deal.
On Monday morning, the prime minister appeared to add more detail, suggesting freedom of movement would only return in the UK having been sanctioned in a referendum.

V2G tech enables drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheaper and then sell some back to the grid at times of high demand 
 
 
Business live – latest updates  




Electric cars that can be used as “power plants on wheels” could be given government backing as part of plans under consideration to help UK manufacturers.
Ministers are considering giving manufacturers incentives to add “vehicle to grid” (V2G) technology to cars as part of its review of the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate.

The technology allows drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheap overnight, and then sell some of it back to the grid at times of high demand.
If millions of cars have the ability to send power back – or power the driver’s home (V2H) – it could help to solve one of the big problems of the transition away from fossil fuels to renewables: how to balance the grid during still, cloudy or dark periods when wind and solar generation is lower than electricity demand.


The move could give incentives to help to spread a technology that is not yet widely used, but which could lessen the load on the grid and the need to fire up expensive gas power plants to fill gaps in supply. Home batteries can do the same job.
Smart charging tariffs, which do not need V2G tech, already help with the opposite problem by encouraging electric vehicle (EV) owners to charge up when electricity is overabundant and cheap – reducing the need to pay renewable generators to switch off.
However, campaign groups said the ZEV incentives could also have the perverse effect of allowing carmakers to sell more polluting petrol models in the next few years.
Carmakers could earn a “credit” for selling cars installed with V2G technology, also known as bidirectional charging, according to plans detailed in a government consultation that closed on Friday. That credit would allow the carmakers to sell another petrol car without facing the risk of fines if they miss the ZEV targets.
The government is preparing to cut electric vehicle sales targets under the ZEV mandate. Environmental groups are braced for changes that could mean an additional 147m tonnes of carbon emitted into the atmosphere by 2050.

A Cabinet battle has erupted over plans to drill at Britain’s largest undeveloped oil and gas field. 
The dispute has placed Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh on opposing sides of a decision that could divide Andy Burnham’s Government.








Mr Healey is backing plans to develop the Rosebank field, which is believed to contain around 500 million barrels of oil, according to The Telegraph.
However, Ms Fahnbulleh, who has formal responsibility for deciding whether the project can proceed, is reportedly leaning towards rejecting the application because of its environmental impact.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is also opposed to the development. He has previously described proposals to extract oil from Rosebank as "climate vandalism" that would damage the Government’s net zero ambitions.
The disagreement leaves the Prime Minister caught between senior members of his Cabinet. Downing Street insisted on Sunday evening that Mr Burnham was not involved in the decision.





John Healey backs Rosebank oil | 
GETTY




Rosebank is located around 80 miles west of the Shetland Islands and is the largest undeveloped oil and gas field in the UK.
Environmental campaigners have warned that developing the site could produce seven times as much carbon dioxide as the Jackdaw gas field east of Aberdeen.
Ms Fahnbulleh approved drilling at Jackdaw this week after deciding that the project would strengthen Britain’s energy security. However, she believes Rosebank presents a different case.
Officials said the Energy Secretary expects most of the oil produced at Rosebank to be sold overseas instead of being used in Britain. She therefore believes the development would do little to improve the country’s energy supply and is leaning towards blocking it.
A decision is expected within the coming weeks.









Ms Fahnbulleh has stressed that the final choice rests with her. Speaking to journalists this week, she said: "Ultimately, only I can make that decision."

Cabinet split emerges over controversial Rosebank oilfield decision


Chancellor is in favour of North Sea project, but energy secretary has said she is leaning towards rejecting it




A cabinet split has emerged over whether to approve drilling at the Rosebank oilfield, with the chancellor, John Healey, in favour of the controversial North Sea project.
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is ultimately in charge of the decision, and the Guardian reported last week that she was leaning towards rejecting it after granting permission for the smaller Jackdaw gasfield.

It is understood, however, that Healey backs approving the licence, which is on hold over concerns about the project’s environmental impact.
The chancellor hinted at his support last week when he told ITV he expected oil and gas revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, suggesting he was anticipating income from Rosebank. The prime minister would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision.
No 10 declined to comment on Sunday after the Mail on Sunday reported that Andy Burnham and Healey had agreed to try to push the project through, saying it was a matter for the energy secretary.

Fahnbulleh is responsible, but the views of Burnham and Healey will hold weight in the choice over whether or not to go ahead.


She told the Guardian the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it.
“One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.”
If the Rosebank field is rejected, it would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners. A final decision is expected before the end of the year.
Labour MPs said on Wednesday that there would be a big pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessary part of the transition to net zero.
MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent.
